edges.description: Microfilarial migration into the skin and the inflammatory response to dying microfilariae produce onchocercal dermatitis.
The inflammatory reaction to microfilariae in the skin drives the severe itching characteristic of onchocerciasis.
Chronic microfilaria-driven dermatitis leads to depigmentation ("leopard skin") changes.
Microfilarial invasion of the cornea provokes inflammatory (sclerosing) keratitis.
Microfilarial invasion and death within the choroid and retina provoke posterior-segment inflammation (chorioretinitis).
Progressive ocular inflammation from microfilarial infiltration culminates in visual loss (river blindness).
The chronic effects of onchocerciasis, including lymphadenitis, follow from ongoing microfilarial degeneration rather than from adult-worm encapsulation.
Wolbachia endosymbiont products amplify the corneal inflammatory response that drives sclerosing keratitis.
Wolbachia-driven inflammatory pathology contributes to posterior-segment chorioretinitis.
Wolbachia-driven inflammatory pathology contributes to progression of onchocercal ocular disease toward blindness.
Encapsulation of coiled adult worms in an outer layer of fibrous scar forms the palpable subcutaneous nodule.

edges.description: Progressive lymphatic fibrosis and obstruction of lymph flow produces adenolymphocele ("hanging groin") and genital elephantiasis.

nodes.description: Adult Onchocerca volvulus worms coil and become encapsulated by host fibrous tissue in subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomata).

Onchocercal ocular disease covers a large spectrum of manifestations, which in severe cases, may lead to blindness.

nodes.description: Posterior-segment inflammation of the choroid and retina; the leading cause of onchocercal blindness. Findings include intraretinal microfilariae, hemorrhages, pigmentary changes, and progressive chorioretinal scarring.

evidence.reference_title: Longitudinal study of lesions of the posterior segment in onchocerciasis.
evidence.snippet: Onchocerciasis is a major cause of blindness, and much of the blindness due to onchocerciasis is caused by chorioretinitis.
Skin symptoms are commonly nonspecific and include severe pruritus, acute and chronic dermatitis

nodes.description: A 6-week course of doxycycline 100 mg/day targets the obligate Wolbachia endosymbionts of Onchocerca volvulus. Wolbachia depletion is macrofilaricidal (sterilizes adult females) and reduces filarial load and ocular disease progression.

evidence.snippet: 100 mg/d of doxycycline for 6 weeks might be effective in reducing the filarial load and preventing ocular symptoms

nodes.description: Adenolymphocele: enlarged, fibrotic inguinal or femoral lymph nodes that come to lie within a pendulous fold of lax, atrophic skin as a consequence of chronic onchocercal lymphadenitis; may be accompanied by elephantiasis of the genitalia.

evidence.reference_title: Pathologic changes of human onchocerciasis: implications for future research.
evidence.snippet: Onchocercal lymphadenitis is characterized initially by histiocytic hyperplasia and follicular atrophy and later by fibrosis and obstruction of lymph flow, a condition causing adenolymphocele ("hanging groin") and elephantiasis of the genitalia.

nodes.description: Inflammatory keratitis caused by microfilarial invasion of the cornea, a leading cause of visual impairment in onchocerciasis.

evidence.snippet: Individual microfilariae in the cornea may be associated with localized punctate lesions or, especially when present in large numbers, may provoke a sclerosing keratitis due to invasion by fibrovascular pannus from the limbal conjunctiva.

nodes.description: Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae migrate from subcutaneous nodules into the skin and anterior chamber of the eye. Their accumulation and death trigger host inflammatory responses causing dermatitis, hypopigmentation, and progressive ocular disease that can advance to blindness.

evidence.snippet: Onchocercal ocular disease covers a large spectrum of manifestations, which in severe cases, may lead to blindness.

nodes.description: Draining lymph nodes respond to microfilaria-driven chronic inflammation with histiocytic hyperplasia and follicular atrophy, progressing to fibrosis that obstructs lymph flow.

nodes.description: Vitiligo-like hypopigmentation with skin atrophy, a classic chronic skin manifestation of onchocerciasis sometimes called "leopard skin."

Onchocerca volvulus harbors obligate Wolbachia endosymbionts that support filarial survival and reproduction and contribute to the severity of host inflammatory pathology. Targeting Wolbachia with doxycycline depletes adult worms and reduces progression of ocular disease.

evidence.snippet: chemotherapeutic approach that targets filarial Wolbachia symbionts in the treatment and control of onchocerciasis, however, suggests that 100 mg/d of doxycycline for 6 weeks might be effective in reducing the filarial load and preventing ocular symptoms
